headline: 4,851 passengers stranded as 28 Dhaka-Saudi flights cancelled
summary: Flight disruptions to Riyadh and Jeddah follow attacks on Saudi airports, including King Khalid International Airport.
details: A total of 28 flights from Dhaka to Riyadh and Jeddah have been cancelled over the last three days, leaving 4,851 passengers stranded at Shahjalal International Airport.
The cancellations include four flights of Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two of US-Bangla, three of Riyadh Air, and 16 transit flights of IndiGo Airlines.
The disruptions are a result of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which were claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group.
According to Saudi authorities, a strike on Saturday killed 12 people, including two Bangladeshis, and injured 309 others.
Reuters reported that 99.7 percent of scheduled flights at the Riyadh airport were cancelled on Sunday, and approximately 60 percent of Monday's flights were also expected to be cancelled.
caption:

headline_marked: US academics [[Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize]] for stabilizing economies
headline: US academics Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize for stabilizing economies
summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for developing models used by central banks globally to manage economic shocks.
details: US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their decades of work developing ground-up models used by central banks and finance ministries worldwide to stabilize economies.
The award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is worth 12 million Swedish crowns, approximately $1.2 million.
The laureates' key insight was that economies are best stabilized by considering the millions of micro-level decisions made by households and businesses, rather than relying on top-down theories.
Michael Woodford, 70, of Columbia University, noted that the new framework was particularly useful during the global financial crisis of the late 2000s to bolster traditional monetary policy tools.
The duo's work promoted essential concepts like 'forward guidance' on interest rate policy and 'sticky' inflation, where price changes lag behind changes in demand.
They also introduced the 'output gap' measure, which helps authorities steer demand pressure in an economy toward zero to maintain stability.
The economics prize, established by Sweden's central bank in 1969, has historically seen a majority of laureates from the United States.
The most recent female winner of the prize was Claudia Goldin in 2023, who was recognized for her work on gender pay and employment gaps in the US.
caption:
Two US academics just won the Nobel Prize in Economics for creating the tools central banks use to save economies from crisis.

US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their decades of work developing ground-up models used by central banks and finance ministries worldwide to stabilize economies.

The award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is worth 12 million Swedish crowns, approximately $1.2 million.

The laureates' key insight was that economies are best stabilized by considering the millions of micro-level decisions made by households and businesses, rather than relying on top-down theories.

Michael Woodford, 70, of Columbia University, noted that the new framework was particularly useful during the global financial crisis of the late 2000s to bolster traditional monetary policy tools.

The duo's work promoted essential concepts like 'forward guidance' on interest rate policy and 'sticky' inflation, where price changes lag behind changes in demand.

They also introduced the 'output gap' measure, which helps authorities steer demand pressure in an economy toward zero to maintain stability.

The economics prize, established by Sweden's central bank in 1969, has historically seen a majority of laureates from the United States.

The most recent female winner of the prize was Claudia Goldin in 2023, who was recognized for her work on gender pay and employment gaps in the US.
